Genesis 1: The account begins before human history. Its seven-day structure ends with the seventh day, when God rested (Genesis 2:2–3).
Genesis 2: The garden is placed "eastward in Eden" (Genesis 2:8), watered by a river that divides into four, including Hiddekel (the Tigris) and Euphrates (Genesis 2:14).
Genesis 3: The scene is the garden in Eden. The chapter ends with the man and woman sent out and cherubims placed at its east side (Genesis 3:24).
Genesis 4: After leaving Eden, Cain settles in the land of Nod, east of Eden, and builds a city named after his son Enoch (Genesis 4:16–17).
Genesis 5: The genealogy runs from Adam to Noah's sons, ten generations, giving each father's age at his son's birth and at his death.
Genesis 6: The chapter is set in the generations before the flood, when Noah was 500 years old or more (Genesis 5:32).
Genesis 7: The flood begins "in the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, the seventeenth day of the month" (Genesis 7:11).
Genesis 8: The ark rests "upon the mountains of Ararat" (Genesis 8:4), a region in eastern Turkey and Armenia known in Assyrian records as Urartu.
Genesis 9: Noah and his sons begin again after the flood. Noah lives 350 years after it (Genesis 9:28).
Genesis 10: The table of nations names peoples across Mesopotamia, Egypt, Canaan, Arabia, and the Mediterranean coasts, descended from Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
Genesis 11: Babel is in "the land of Shinar" (Genesis 11:2), southern Mesopotamia. Terah's family moves from Ur of the Chaldees, a major Sumerian city on the Euphrates, to Haran in upper Mesopotamia.
Genesis 12: Abram leaves Haran at age seventy-five (Genesis 12:4) for Canaan, then goes to Egypt in a famine. The patriarchs are traditionally dated to the early second millennium BC; no record outside the Bible names them.
Genesis 13: Abram and Lot separate near Bethel. Lot chooses the Jordan plain near Sodom; Abram settles by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron (Genesis 13:18).
Genesis 14: Four eastern kings, led by Chedorlaomer of Elam, campaign against five cities of the Jordan plain. Abram pursues them north to Dan and Hobah, near Damascus.
Genesis 15: God makes a covenant with Abram, promising land "from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates" (Genesis 15:18).
Genesis 16: Hagar's son Ishmael is born when Abram is eighty-six (Genesis 16:16), ten years after Abram settled in Canaan.
Genesis 17: Abram is ninety-nine when God changes his name to Abraham and gives circumcision as the covenant sign (Genesis 17:1, 24).
Genesis 18: Abraham is camped by the oaks of Mamre near Hebron. From there he looks toward Sodom in the Jordan plain.
Genesis 19: Sodom and Gomorrah were cities of the plain near the Dead Sea. Lot flees to the small town of Zoar.
Genesis 20: Abraham stays in Gerar, in the western Negev between Kadesh and Shur (Genesis 20:1).
Genesis 21: Isaac is born when Abraham is a hundred (Genesis 21:5). Abraham makes a treaty with Abimelech at Beersheba in the Negev.
Genesis 22: Abraham travels three days from Beersheba to "the land of Moriah" (Genesis 22:2). 2 Chronicles 3:1 names mount Moriah as the site of Solomon's temple.
Genesis 23: Sarah dies at 127 in Hebron (Genesis 23:1–2). Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah from Ephron the Hittite.
Genesis 24: Abraham's servant travels to the city of Nahor in Mesopotamia (Genesis 24:10), several hundred miles north of Hebron, to find a wife for Isaac.
Genesis 25: Abraham dies at 175 (Genesis 25:7). Isaac is sixty when Esau and Jacob are born (Genesis 25:26).
Genesis 26: During a famine Isaac stays in Gerar, then moves to Beersheba. Esau marries two Hittite women at forty (Genesis 26:34).
Genesis 27: Isaac is old and blind (Genesis 27:1). The family is living at Beersheba (Genesis 28:10).
Genesis 28: Jacob travels from Beersheba toward Haran and stops at Luz, which he renames Bethel (Genesis 28:19), in the central hill country.
Genesis 29: Jacob reaches Haran and serves Laban seven years for Rachel, then seven more (Genesis 29:20, 30).
Genesis 30: Jacob's children are born in Haran over the years he works for Laban.
Genesis 31: After twenty years with Laban (Genesis 31:38), Jacob flees toward Canaan. Laban overtakes him in the hills of Gilead, east of the Jordan.
Genesis 32: Jacob camps at Mahanaim and wrestles at the ford of Jabbok, a tributary that flows into the Jordan from the east.
Genesis 33: Jacob meets Esau, then builds a house at Succoth and buys land near Shechem (Genesis 33:17–19).
Genesis 34: The events take place at Shechem, a city in the central hill country between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim.
Genesis 35: Jacob returns to Bethel. Rachel dies on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem (Genesis 35:19), and Isaac dies at Hebron aged 180.
Genesis 36: Esau's descendants settle in mount Seir, the land of Edom, southeast of the Dead Sea. The list includes kings who reigned in Edom before Israel had a king (Genesis 36:31).
Genesis 37: Joseph is seventeen (Genesis 37:2). His brothers sell him at Dothan to Ishmaelites carrying spices to Egypt.
Genesis 38: Judah separates from his brothers and settles near Adullam, in the lowland of Judah. Timnath, where Tamar meets him, is nearby.
Genesis 39: Joseph serves in Egypt in the house of Potiphar, "an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard" (Genesis 39:1).
Genesis 40: Joseph is about twenty-eight, some years after being sold into Egypt, and is held in the prison "where the king's prisoners were bound" (Genesis 39:20). He is thirty when he stands before Pharaoh two years later (Genesis 41:1, 46).
Genesis 41: Joseph is thirty when he stands before Pharaoh (Genesis 41:46). Egypt's harvests depended on the yearly Nile flood.
Genesis 42: Famine reaches Canaan, and Jacob sends ten sons to buy grain in Egypt.
Genesis 43: The famine continues in its second year (Genesis 45:6), and the brothers return to Egypt with Benjamin.
Genesis 44: Joseph's steward overtakes the brothers on their way home from Egypt.
Genesis 45: Joseph reveals himself in the second year of the famine, with five years still to come (Genesis 45:6).
Genesis 46: Jacob leaves Beersheba with his family—seventy persons in all (Genesis 46:27)—and settles in the land of Goshen in the eastern Nile Delta.
Genesis 47: Jacob is 130 when he meets Pharaoh (Genesis 47:9). The family lives "in the land of Rameses" (Genesis 47:11).
Genesis 48: Jacob, near death in Egypt, blesses Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh.
Genesis 49: Jacob speaks to his twelve sons and dies in Egypt at 147 (Genesis 47:28).
Genesis 50: Jacob is buried in the cave of Machpelah at Hebron. Joseph dies in Egypt at 110 (Genesis 50:26).
